title: Jimbo Fisher wants back into coaching: ‘If I can recruit without money, I can recruit with money’
content:
CHARLOTTE — Jimbo Fisher enjoys his new life on camera. He’s spent most of this week on set as part of the ACC Network’s coverage of the league’s media days.

“But coaches are coaches,” Fisher told The Athletic on Friday. And he’d still like to scribble out “television analyst” on his business cards and replace it with “head coach.”

Fisher would love to get back into coaching, even as the sport he left after the 2023 season has plunged into chaos with an uncertain, ever-changing rulebook.

“The relationship with players. The competition. I miss the competition. I miss recruiting. If I can recruit without money, I can recruit with money. I promise you that,” Fisher said. “But I miss the competition, the gameplanning. That was never work to me. That was fun. It was a grind, but it was fun.”

Fisher spent a decade as an assistant coach under Nick Saban and Bobby Bowden at LSU and Florida State before taking over in Tallahassee in 2010. He went 83-23 and won the 2013 season’s national title with quarterback Jameis Winston in the middle of a run of three consecutive ACC titles.

With the Seminoles scuffling at 5-6 in 2017, he left for Texas A&M and signed an unprecedented fully guaranteed 10-year contract worth $75 million. After going 9-1 in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, he signed an extension that guaranteed him $95 million. He went 8-4 in 2021, 5-7 in 2022 and was 6-4 late in the 2023 season when Texas A&M paid him $77.5 millon — the largest buyout in college football history — to fire him and hire Mike Elko, who led Texas A&M to the College Football Playoff last season.

Now, Fisher says he participates weekly in The 33rd Team, a weekly call started in 2019 by former New York Jets general manager Mike Tannenbaum in which former coaches, general managers and players discuss the sport. The 33rd Team has also consulted with teams making hires.

Fisher said he’d be open to joining a college program or NFL franchise as an offensive coordinator if he felt the fit was right.

But what’s the right fit as a head coach?

“Anyone that would give us a fair chance to win,” Fisher said. “It doesn’t have to be elite-elite. I’ve coached in different levels, (FCS), Cincinnati, different places. It’s just coaching ball.”

Preparing for a college football Saturday with ACC Network scratches the same gameplanning itch for Fisher that used to take up his time during his more than three decades as a coach.

“It feels like you’re right back on the sideline again,” Fisher said.

He added he’s thought about how he would set up a front office as the money allocated to players has exploded since his exit from the sport and general managers have become commonplace.

“There’s a place for pro football in that realm and a place for college football,” he said. “GMs and people aren’t used to recruiting. There’s an art to recruiting and how you go about recruiting and setting that process up. There’s a division within that. There’s a group that handles money and disperses. There’s evaluators, recruiters and money dispersers and the head coach has got to still have that power over that as he goes.”

For now, Fisher is prepared for his third season away from the sport and another spent behind a desk on camera.

“If another opportunity doesn’t come, I like doing TV,” he said. “I like the people, the interaction. I like it.”
